alternative: Serialize per key with an async mutex (a Map<Key, Promise> chain, the async-mutex package, or a keyed-lock helper) and use the Web Locks API where the runtime exposes navigator.locks; treat SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics.wait/notify as a worker-only mechanism, not as the default design.
idiom_name: per-key async mutex / Web Locks named locks instead of striped locks
implementation_notes: TypeScript runs on the same single-threaded event loop as JavaScript, so striped OS locks are neither available nor meaningful on the main thread; the equivalent problem is serializing interleaved async work per key, solved with a Map<Key, Promise> chain or an async-mutex keyed by entity id, typed so that the critical section can only run through the helper. In Node, worker_threads share memory only through SharedArrayBuffer, where Atomics.wait/notify implement a real lock inside a worker; browsers and workers can use the Web Locks API (navigator.locks.request), whose named locks behave like platform-managed, unbounded stripes. Use a real mutex only inside workers, never as the primary application design.
pitfalls: A keyed promise chain leaks entries unless drained ones are deleted, and an unhandled rejection can poison every later operation on that key.
TypeScript's types cannot express lock ownership: an awaited operation that escapes the critical section will not be caught, so keep the lock acquisition inside the helper that also awaits the work.
Web Locks require a secure context and are origin-scoped, and Node has no navigator.locks - feature-detect and fall back to promise chaining.
